name: Kernel-based Resampling

# Kernel-based Resampling
## Overview
Kernel-based resampling approximates a continuous volumetric field $V(\mathbf{p})$ from discrete samples $V_i$ by convolving the data with a spatially localized weight function (kernel) centered at the query position $\mathbf{p}$ along the viewing ray [G]. It solves the discretization artifacts inherent in [nearest-neighbor sampling](#1151-nearest-neighbor-density-lookup.md) by providing a continuous, differentiable estimate of the volume value [G]. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like [Nearest Neighbor Sampling](11694-nearest-neighbor-sampling.md) by utilizing multiple neighbors to reduce aliasing, and from [Linear Interpolation](14935-linear-interpolation.md) by relying on higher-order kernels for sharper frequency response [G].
## Shared principles
This family inherits the core mechanism from [Interpolation Methods](10526-interpolation-methods.md), which covers query positioning, kernel weight application, and coordinate transformation [G].
## Subtopics

### [Interpolation Schemes for Volume Rendering](817-interpolation-schemes-for-volume-rendering.md)
Approximates a continuous scalar field from discrete voxel samples to determine values at arbitrary query positions along viewing rays. Sets itself apart by encompassing the full spectrum from zero-order box filters to high-order frequency-domain sinc resampling, including specialized hardware approximations and fast GPU-accelerated cubic evaluations. Chosen when a broad range of fidelity and performance trade-offs is needed.

### [Lanczos Resampling](11246-lanczos-resampling.md)
Resamples volumetric data by replacing each selected sample with a translated copy of the [Lanczos kernel](#11246-lanczos-resampling.md), a limited Sinc function. Distinguishes itself from siblings by using a windowed sinc function that balances sharpness with the suppression of ringing artifacts compared to a pure [sinc filter](#2085-ideal-low-pass-filter-rect-filter.md). Chosen when higher fidelity than linear or cubic interpolation is required, particularly in medical imaging contexts where preserving high-frequency details during [compression](#4-compression.md) or reconstruction is critical.

### [Interpolation Functions for Resampling](15932-interpolation-functions-for-resampling.md)
Defines the mathematical kernels used to estimate continuous volume values from discrete samples for edge reconstruction and shading. Distinguished from sibling methods by its specific focus on the trade-off between grey-value reconstruction fidelity and edge location accuracy, particularly in medical imaging contexts where negative values or gradient errors produce visible artifacts. Chosen when edge location accuracy is paramount.

### [Windowed Sinc Interpolation](18705-windowed-sinc-interpolation.md)
Approximates a continuous [volume function](#21847-volumetric-representation.md) by convolving discrete voxel samples with a truncated sinc kernel modulated by a window function, primarily to reduce aliasing artifacts inherent in ideal sinc interpolation while maintaining high frequency response. Distinguished from its siblings by its explicit support for [anisotropic voxel](#2552-voxel-cone-tracing-anisotropic-filtering.md) resampling via a directional blur factor, making it particularly suitable for converting anisotropic medical imaging data (e.g., breast tomosynthesis) into isotropic grids for volume rendering. Chosen when anisotropic data requires [isotropic resampling](#7482-volume-resampling-to-isotropic-spacing.md).

## Background
Kernel-based resampling is a fundamental technique in digital signal processing and computer graphics, rooted in the Whittaker–Shannon interpolation formula which states that a band-limited signal can be perfectly reconstructed from its samples using a sinc kernel [G]. In volume rendering, exact sinc reconstruction is computationally prohibitive due to its infinite support, leading to the development of truncated and windowed kernels (such as Lanczos) and polynomial approximations (such as B-splines) [G]. The method is widely used in [direct volume ray casting](#19-direct-volume-ray-casting.md) to ensure smooth visual transitions and accurate [gradient estimation](#6476-gradient-estimation-our-grad.md) for lighting calculations [G].
